TITLE: Leverage KernelSHAP: An Adversarial Version of LeverageSHAP for KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We propose Leverage KernelSHAP, an algorithm for providing non-asymptotic guarantees for KernelSHAP. This algorithm is based on the idea that the rows of the kernel-weighted design matrix are sampled according to their statistical leverage scores. Specifically, we consider an adversarial setting where the user seeks to guarantee that the solution returned by KernelSHAP satisfies a certain desired accuracy even when facing an adversary selecting the true target $\bm{\phi}^*$ in the worst possible way. 
We leverage the same sampling strategy used in LeverageSHAP but now applied in the constrained least-squares regression problem of KernelSHAP. We will study the properties of this new method and evaluate its performance through simulations on some public datasets (MNIST, CIFAR) and comparisons against LeverageSHAP.
CONTROLS: We compare Leverage KernelSHAP with original KernelSHAP, LeverageSHAP and unbiased KernelSHAP on synthetic and real-world data. We also investigate the robustness to various parameters and hyperparameter settings.
COST: 450000
PREDICTION: Leverage KernelSHAP might outperform the state-of-the-art methods for KernelSHAP and related estimators, especially in cases where the input dimension is high. However, its actual performance may heavily depend on the hyperparameters and may exhibit computational efficiency issues for large scale problems.

TITLE: Understanding the Effect of Sampling Distributions on KernelSHAP
PROPOSAL: We investigate how different sampling distributions affect the quality of the KernelSHAP estimator, by deriving new bounds for KernelSHAP using a variety of sampling strategies, including direct sampling, pairing, and replacement. The primary goal of this investigation is to provide an in-depth analysis of which sampling scheme works best with which types of models and datasets.
Specifically, we derive concentration inequalities for the KernelSHAP estimator when using different sampling strategies, and compare the results. This analysis aims at determining whether the choice of sampling distribution impacts the performance of KernelSHAP, particularly with respect to the notion of  ``best" random subsample distribution so that the least-squares objective can be written as an expectation with respect to this sampling distribution.
CONTROLS: We compare the bounds for different sampling distributions with each other, as well as with current experimental results on various real and synthetic datasets (CIFAR-10, CelebA, Adult dataset, for instance). We will further investigate the convergence of the lower bounds with respect to the variance of the sampling distribution.

TITLE: Coreset-Based Approximation for High-Dimensional Shapley Values
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel technique for approximating Shapley values in high-dimensional data using coresets, which are small, weighted subsets of the data that preserve the key characteristics of the original dataset. PROPOSAL: We will compare the ability of two types of models to forecast future satellite images while maintaining consistency with observed temporal patterns: DeepRNNs (fine-tuned on satellite image forecasting) and diffusion-based image generators (conditioned on temporal cues from historical images). TITLE:  Multi-Step Forecasting with Adaptive Attention 
PROPOSAL: We develop an online forecasting method, dubbed OAA-TS (Online Attention Adaptation for Time Series), that leverages an attention mechanism to selectively focus on the most relevant information for multi-step forecasting. TITLE:  Learning From Distributionally Robust Observations
PROPOSAL: We introduce a novel online time series forecasting method, called DRofi (Distributional Robustness from Firsthand Observations). DRofi aims to learn a robust forecasting model that can accurately predict future values even when the underlying distribution of the data has shifted. To achieve this, DRofi formulates the forecasting problem as a distributionally robust optimization (DRO) problem, where the goal is to find a model that minimizes the loss under the worst-case distribution within a given set. DRofi uses a two-step approach: first, it predicts the distribution of the future observations using a density estimation model; second, it optimizes the forecasting model to be robust against the predicted distribution. TITLE:  Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks for Online Time Series Forecasting
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to online time series forecasting using Temporal Graph Convolutional Networks (TGCNs). TGCNs can model complex relationships between time series data and leverage graph structure to capture spatial and temporal correlations.
